title: Bitcoin Faces Pressure After Fed’s Hawkish Rate Hold
text:
Traders are pricing in a 78% chance of a December rate hike, while analysts say Treasury yields, the US dollar and upcoming inflation data could determine Bitcoin’s next move.
Bitcoin could face further headwinds after the US Federal Reserve held interest rates steady while signaling continued concern about inflation, according to market analysts.
The Fed voted 10-2 Wednesday to maintain its benchmark interest rate at 3.75% to 4%, with Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack favoring a quarter-point increase.
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh acknowledged that inflation remained above the central bank’s 2% target.
“Americans… are still dealing with inflation that has been running above the Committee’s objective for close to 6 years. It’s our responsibility to get inflation down,” he said.
Iggy Ioppe, chief investment officer at tokenization platform Theo, said the decision itself was widely expected, but investors had not fully anticipated the Fed’s hawkish messaging.
“Markets had the hold priced, but not the hawkish tone,” he said in comments sent to Cointelegraph.
There are expectations that the Fed will raise rates in its Dec. 8-9 meeting, and again next year.
CME FedWatch data showed traders assigning a 78.4% probability to a quarter-point increase by December and a 67.3% probability of at least a quarter-point increase by March, as of Wednesday.
Warsh declined to say whether the Fed would raise rates at the end of the year.
“A lot of things can happen, so I’m not going to be able to share with you my musings about what happens when this group gets together six weeks from now,” he said during a press conference.
At elevated interest rates, Bitcoin has to “compete with” a risk-free rate near 4%, said Ioppe.
Related: Bitcoin price bounce rejected at 50-day trend line ahead of FOMC, earnings
However, Bitget analyst Lewis Huang said Bitcoin’s next move could depend less on the Fed’s decision itself than on Treasury yields, the US dollar and broader investor sentiment.
“With limited new direction from the Fed, Bitcoin’s near-term performance may depend more heavily on Treasury yields, dollar movements and broader risk sentiment,” he said.
Analysts, including Huang, are now looking to Thursday’s personal consumption expenditures inflation report and earnings from major technology companies for clues about the direction of risk assets.
Sygnum Bank chief investment officer Fabian Dori agreed, adding that “the next couple of days promise more excitement” with Thursday’s release of PCE inflation data.
“Various Mag 7 companies reporting earnings this week will help clarify whether AI capex is turning into revenues. Following these short-term catalysts, broader liquidity and financial conditions are likely to shape the path towards the December decision,” he added.

title: Tampered Ledger Wallets Cost Singapore Users $2.7M
text:
Police say at least two cases were reported as early as Sept. 10, nearly a month before the wider incident became public.
Singapore police say at least two cases involving tampered Ledger hardware wallets have been reported since Sept. 10, with combined losses of about 3.5 million Singapore dollars ($2.7 million), placing local reports almost a month before the wider incident became public.
In an advisory published Wednesday, the Singapore Police Force said preliminary investigations found malicious hardware components in Ledger wallets purchased from some retail stores in Singapore.
The disclosure adds both a local loss figure and an earlier reporting date to the incident, which surfaced publicly on Oct. 9 following reports of losses involving devices sold through CryptoBilis, an authorized Ledger reseller in Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines.
Days later, former Mt. Gox CEO Mark Karpelès said that a Ledger Flex purchased at Singapore’s airport contained a spy implant.
Another Ledger user claimed to have a tampered device bought from local IT retailer Challenger. The user said he was later sent a new device from Ledger.
On Oct. 13, Ledger said it has asked retailers in Indonesia, Singapore, Thailand, the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia, and Hong Kong to suspend sales of Ledger devices as investigations are ongoing.
Singapore police said it is in contact with Ledger, which is reviewing the affected cases, while police investigations are ongoing.

title: CFTC Chair Says Fridges Could Stake Ether, Launch Memecoins
text:
CFTC chair Mike Selig says autonomous AI agents could challenge financial rules built around human traders, and regulators need to adapt.
Commodity Futures Trading Commission Chair Michael Selig says it is “no longer science fiction” to imagine one’s refrigerator autonomously purchasing groceries with money earned from staking Ether — or even launching its own memecoin, raising questions about how regulators should oversee autonomous AI agents.
The colorful comment came during Selig’s remarks at the CFTC’s inaugural Frontier Forum in Washington, DC, on Wednesday, where he argued that regulators must adapt to a financial system where AI agents can hold assets and execute trades autonomously.
“We’re gathered here today to discuss a technology that’s rapidly transforming the financial markets. President Trump calls it ‘super intelligence,’ or SI, because ‘it’s not artificial.’ It’s as real as the printing press, the steam engine, and the internet,” he said.
Selig says the CFTC’s regulatory framework was developed around “identifiable market participants” performing specific financial functions, but autonomous software is raising questions about how those rules apply.
“Consider an SI agent that identifies trading opportunities and executes transactions on behalf of a user,” said Selig.
“Does the developer of that agent become subject to registration? Who is liable if the agent goes rogue? How can regulators know who the agent, or suite of agents, is trading on behalf of? Do we need a new flavor of know-your-customer, maybe KYA or know-your-agent?”
Selig said AI could give smaller traders and businesses access to risk-management that was once reserved for larger institutions.
“SI can help process the vast amount of information significantly faster than human brain power and with greater accuracy,” he said.
But greater autonomy also comes with new risks. Agents could react unexpectedly to market conditions, while those using similar models could generate correlated trading behavior. The speed of autonomous transactions could also complicate market surveillance and risk management, he said.
Related: Coinbase CEO touts agentic finance as Base tops 100M AI payments
Animoca Brands Chairman Yat Siu recently raised a similar concern, telling Cointelegraph that a thousand people asking AI about the same trade could receive roughly the same answer. Users’ own knowledge and follow-up questions help shape more personalized strategies, he said.
Last year, the Bank of England’s Financial Policy Committee also warned that widespread use of similar models could amplify market shocks.
Crypto exchanges are already developing tools for autonomous trading.
Coinbase introduced Agentic Wallets in February, allowing agents to spend and trade within user-defined limits, while Binance launched AI Agent Skills in March to provide market data and tools for placing and managing spot orders.

Bitcoin ETFs Add $137M as October Inflows Turn Positive
text:
Bitcoin ETFs drew $424 million over three days, lifting October net inflows to $111 million despite a hawkish Federal Reserve decision and weaker crypto sentiment.
US-listed spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) extended their daily inflow streak to three on Wednesday, pushing October back into positive territory with two trading sessions left in the month.
Bitcoin (BTC) ETFs attracted $137 million on Wednesday, bringing their three-day inflows to roughly $424 million and October’s net inflows to $111 million, according to SoSoValue data.
October’s cumulative net flows remained negative through Tuesday, after nearly $774 million flowed out over the final two trading days of the previous week.
The Bitcoin ETF rebound coincided with the US Federal Reserve keeping its benchmark interest rate unchanged at a target range of 3.75% to 4% on Wednesday. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh warned that inflation remained above the central bank’s 2% target.
“With limited new direction from the Fed, Bitcoin’s near-term performance may depend more heavily on Treasury yields, dollar movements and broader risk sentiment,” Bitget analyst Lewis Huang said.
Bitcoin traded at $79,848 at the time of writing, down around 1% over the past 24 hours, according to CoinGecko. Market sentiment remained unchanged, with the Crypto Fear & Greed Index holding at 51, or “Neutral,” for a second consecutive day.
Meanwhile, Ether (ETH) ETFs continued to see withdrawals, shedding another $21 million on Wednesday and bringing October’s net outflows to $1.35 billion. Ether traded at $2,310, down 1.7% over the past 24 hours.

title: ECB President Christine Lagarde to Step Down in February 2027
text:
Lagarde announced plans to step down as European Central Bank President after serving more than seven years in the role.
European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde announced plans to step down from her role at the central bank.
“I have just informed my colleagues that I will step down as @ECB President on 7 February 2027,” Lagarde said in a Thursday post on X.
Lagarde became ECB president in November 2019 and will have served for about seven years and three months when she leaves office.

title: Bitcoin Faces Sell-Side Risk Above $85,000, Glassnode Analysis Warns
text:
BTC price analysis from Glassnode drew attention to $85,000 as the lower boundary of a cost-basis zone for long-term holders.
Bitcoin (BTC) faces resistance between $84,000 and $85,000 as analysis points to coins largely linked to a single large holder.
In the latest edition of its regular newsletter, The Week Onchain, crypto analytics platform Glassnode flagged another resistance hurdle for BTC price action in the mid-$80,000 range.
On Nov. 22, 2025, a significant portion of the total BTC supply moved onchain. At the time of the transactions, BTC/USD traded between $84,000 and $85,000. The coins that last moved at that price make up 4.3% of the total BTC supply, or 864,520 BTC.
The analysis links the majority of this Bitcoin to a single large holder, who was moving funds among multiple wallets. Although self-transfers generally do not affect price, Glassnode noted that Bitcoin has respected the $84,000-$85,000 range as both support and resistance over the past 11 months.
“It held as support in December, when price bounced off it on December 1 and December 18. It gave way on January 31, when a push back up to $84K failed, and Bitcoin fell about 20% over the following days,” Glassnode commented.
In May, September and October, BTC price upside momentum faded near the same level, with a high of $87,400. Bitcoin has recorded only five daily closes above the band, never more than three in a row.
“A run of daily closes above $85K would turn the band back into support,” Glassnode added.
BTC/USD chart with supply onchain cost-basis data. Source: Glassnode
The $85,000 mark holds significance for a larger portion of the Bitcoin investor base.
Related: Bitcoin price analysis sees ‘strong rally’ as old coins become dormant
Glassnode reports that Bitcoin’s long-term holders (LTH) — entities holding a given amount of BTC without selling for at least 155 days — own around 4 million coins that last moved onchain between $85,000 and $118,000, mostly in 2025.
“More than half of all their coins were bought above today’s price. If price recovers toward $85K, many of these holders may sell to get their money back,” it said of the LTH cohort as a whole.
Bitcoin supply data by investor cohort. Source: Glassnode
The LTH spent output profit ratio (SOPR), which compares the extent to which LTH coins moving onchain are doing so at a higher or lower price compared to their previous transaction, currently sits at 0.99. Values below 1 imply that LTH supply is moving at an aggregate loss.

Utah Files Felony Charges Against Kalshi, Co-Founders Over Sports Bets - Decrypt
text:
Utah has filed criminal charges against prediction market Kalshi and its two co-founders, accusing them of illegally promoting gambling in the state, ABC4 reported on Wednesday.
KalshiEX LLC, CEO Tarek Mansour and COO Luana Lopes Lara face one count of pattern of unlawful activity, a second-degree felony, 12 counts of online gambling promotion, a third-degree felony, and one count of gambling promotion, a misdemeanor, according to the charging documents.
"Gambling is illegal in Utah, whether you place the bet, run the game, or promote it. Calling it a 'prediction market' doesn't change what it is, and being federally registered doesn't put a company above the law," Utah Attorney General Derek Brown said in a statement.
According to the charges, a special agent with the Utah State Bureau of Investigation set up an undercover account as a Utah resident and placed 12 wagers on sports including NFL and college games in September, passing a location check that confirmed he was in the state. Kalshi earned proceeds from the fees it charged on each bet, prosecutors allege.
Brown's office did not say what penalties it would seek, though the felony charges carry the possibility of jail time, the Associated Press reported.
"This is a crazy overreach; Utah is clearly playing politics," Kalshi said in a statement. "We look forward to putting a stop to this in court, just like we did in Arizona."
The charges escalate a dispute that already involves the federal government. Utah, where the state constitution bans gambling, sued Kalshi in state court last week. On Tuesday, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission sued Utah to block its enforcement actions against CFTC-registered exchanges, making it the 10th state the agency has taken to court.
"Congress entrusted the CFTC to be the federal regulator with sole responsibility to oversee these markets," CFTC Chairman Michael Selig said.
Utah has already won one round. In August, U.S. District Judge Robert Shelby rejected Kalshi's own bid to block enforcement, ruling that federal law "does not preempt Utah's ability to enforce its anti-gambling laws." Kalshi is appealing to the Tenth Circuit, which denied its request for an injunction in September.
President Donald Trump has backed the CFTC, saying in May that it was "critically important that the CFTC's exclusive authority over Prediction Markets is maintained," and calling several state officials who had challenged the platforms "scum."
Federal appeals courts have split on whether states can apply gambling laws to prediction markets. The Third Circuit ruled in April that New Jersey cannot regulate sports contracts on the platforms, while the Sixth and Ninth Circuits sided with Ohio, Tennessee and Nevada in August and September. New Jersey has asked the Supreme Court to settle the question, backed by 39 other states and the District of Columbia.
"Different judges in different places say different things," Isaac Rose-Berman, a gambling policy fellow at the American Institute for Boys and Men, told ABC4. "It's just going to keep escalating and eventually get to the Supreme Court."

title: Treasury Sanctions 11 Over North Korean IT Worker Scheme That Moved Millions in Crypto - Decrypt
text:
The U.S. Treasury Department has sanctioned 10 individuals and one entity for their roles in North Korean IT worker schemes that defraud U.S. businesses and generate revenue for the country's weapons programs, the department said on Wednesday.
North Korea uses fake documents, stolen identities and invented personas to place IT workers at legitimate companies, then takes most of their wages, generating hundreds of millions of dollars for its weapons of mass destruction and ballistic missile programs, according to Treasury. The networks have used "sophisticated cryptocurrency transactions," money laundering and artificial intelligence tools to move millions of dollars to the regime, it said.
Today, Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control sanctioned 10 individuals and one entity for their roles in Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) government-run IT worker schemes that defraud U.S. businesses and generate revenue for the DPRK’s unlawful weapons of mass…
— Treasury Department (@USTreasury) October 28, 2026
"The North Korean regime continues targeting and exploiting American companies through fraudulent activities conducted by its overseas IT operatives, who weaponize sensitive data and extort businesses for substantial payments," said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
Two Russian nationals are among those sanctioned. Vitold Obertas, a Russian intermediary for North Korean financial transactions, has carried out nearly $2 million in crypto conversions since January 2025, plus at least $1.25 million in other currency transactions, for North Korean officials, Treasury said. Ilya Boykov has exchanged and converted the equivalent of $3.5 million in crypto since 2024 for Limited Liability Company Alis, a North Korean IT worker company sanctioned in 2024.
The sanctions listings include two Ethereum and two Tron addresses for Boykov, and one Ethereum and three Tron addresses for Obertas. One Ethereum address appears on both men's entries.
Treasury also sanctioned the First Financial and Technical Development Center, a North Korean-controlled entity based in Vladivostok, Russia, that it said deploys highly trained IT workers who use AI tools and "complex cryptocurrency transfers" to generate revenue. Six Russia-based North Korean IT workers have generated more than $750,000 for the center since 2025, according to Treasury.
Two North Korean nationals who lead Russia-based IT worker delegations were also sanctioned. One of them, Kim Ki Hyok, has transferred nearly $500,000 in crypto for his delegation since 2024, Treasury said.
The action builds on sanctions against a separate North Korean IT worker network in March, and Australia and the European Union have made their own designations this month, according to Treasury.
North Korean IT workers have increasingly targeted crypto projects. In April 2025, Google's Threat Intelligence Group reported that such workers had embedded themselves in crypto projects in the UK, Germany, Portugal and Serbia, including Solana smart contract development, with some operating under as many as 12 fake identities at once.
North Korean hackers have also used long-running deception campaigns against crypto firms. In April, Solana-based exchange Drift Protocol said the attack that drained about $285 million from its platform was a six-month operation by a North Korean state-affiliated group, whose intermediaries met Drift contributors in person and posed as a quantitative trading firm, Decrypt reported.

title: EU Investors Rank Crypto Above Pensions as Lasting Wealth Tools: OKX Survey
text:
European investors ranked crypto above retirement plans for lasting wealth creation, while prior surveys show US investors are skeptical on crypto’s role in retirement accounts.
Investors in several of Europe’s biggest economies ranked crypto above retirement plans as lasting wealth creation tools, with 19% of those surveyed choosing cryptocurrencies, while 8% opted for traditional retirement plans.
US investors still preferred traditional retirement plans, with 21% choosing retirement accounts while only 12% opted for cryptocurrencies, according to a Thursday OKX survey of 1,932 adults age 18 to 88 who previously invested in crypto. The survey was conducted by Pollfish between Oct. 14 and Oct. 18 across the US, France, Germany, the Netherlands and Poland.
Real estate was the top choice for lasting wealth, with 34% of all respondents choosing the broad class above digital assets and retirement accounts, as the asset most associated with lasting wealth.
Younger Europeans have previously shown concerns about whether their retirement plans will provide sufficient income. About 43% of 2,000 surveyed Europeans age 18 to 35 expected their pensions to fall short, according to a May 2026 survey by Friends of Europe’s citizen-engagement unit, Debating Europe.
“When investors under 45 on both sides of the Atlantic treat crypto as part of their long-term wealth, it tells you crypto is now part of how people look at their finances,” said OKX Europe’s CEO, Erald Ghoo. He said that crypto’s place in the wealth plan will become “more important” as these investors get older and wealthier.
Nearly half of European investors, 47%, expect to increase their holdings, including 13% planning a significant increase. Across all age groups, 51% expect to increase their crypto allocation. Boomers are the exception, with 55% saying crypto is not important to generational wealth.
Excluding boomers, US investors generally are more bullish on cryptocurrency’s place in their portfolio, with 55% of surveyed participants expecting to increase their allocation in the next five years and 22% planning a significant increase.
Still, American boomers were more pessimistic about crypto, with 65% saying that crypto was not at all important for generational wealth building, compared to 44% of boomers in Europe.
Related: Settlement concerns prompt Euronext to halt CoinShares’ Zcash ETP ahead of debut
To be sure, Americans are also more skeptical about crypto’s place in retirement accounts. An August survey from The National Institute on Retirement Security found that 77% of Americans consider crypto in workplace retirement plans risky, including 46% who view it as very risky.
Earlier, however, the Trump administration took steps toward broadening access to alternative assets in retirement plans. In May 2025, the US Department of Labor rescinded crypto-specific guidance that had urged 401(k) plan fiduciaries to exercise “extreme care” when considering cryptocurrency investments, returning instead to a neutral approach that neither endorses nor discourages crypto.
In August 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies to expand access to alternative assets in 401(k) plans, including exposure to digital assets through certain investment vehicles.
In March 2026, the US Department of Labor issued a draft proposal seeking to expand investment options in 401(k) retirement plans to include crypto and alternative investments.
In June 2026, SenatorsBernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren and Representative Bobby Scott urged the US Department of Labor to withdraw its proposal to allow digital assets in retirement plans, arguing that the policy would “expose retirement accounts to exceptionally volatile assets, like digital currency.”

title: Coinbase Files for Brazil Crypto License Ahead of Deadline
text:
Coinbase has applied for authorization ahead of Brazil’s Oct. 30 deadline and says it expects to maintain existing services while regulators review its application.
Coinbase has applied for authorization to operate as a crypto service provider in Brazil ahead of the country’s license application deadline on Friday.
The US-based cryptocurrency exchange submitted its application to the Central Bank of Brazil on Wednesday under the country’s virtual asset service provider (VASP) framework, according to a statement shared with Cointelegraph.
The filing aims to maintain Coinbase’s existing Brazilian operations as the central bank introduces new requirements covering governance, customer asset safeguards and compliance.
“We do not expect the application review to require a suspension of our existing services,” a Coinbase spokesperson told Cointelegraph.
Coinbase also reiterated plans to bring its “Everything Exchange” strategy to Brazil, potentially expanding into foreign exchange and payments alongside crypto services. Those activities require separate regulatory authorizations.
Coinbase joins Binance, which applied for authorization on Oct. 23 but has restricted crypto lending, margin trading and other services in Brazil while delisting 22 crypto assets to comply with the new rules.
Brazil requires existing crypto service providers to apply for authorization by the end of October to continue operating under transitional arrangements. Existing providers that apply by the deadline can continue operating while their applications are reviewed.

title: RootstockLabs Sees New Financial Role for Bitcoin
text:
A new report argues that putting institutional Bitcoin holdings to work through lending, collateral and financing could create demand beyond its store-of-value role.
A new report from Bitcoin infrastructure developer RootstockLabs argues that Bitcoin’s next wave of institutional demand could come from lending, yield generation and balance-sheet financing, expanding its role beyond a store of value.
RootstockLabs estimates that just 1.5% of Bitcoin’s (BTC) supply currently participates in lending and Bitcoin-native finance, while identifiable institutional investors hold roughly 3.9 million BTC. Putting more of those holdings to work could create additional demand for the asset without changing its fixed supply.
The analysis identifies two emerging sources of financial utility: generating returns from existing Bitcoin holdings through lending and structured credit, and using Bitcoin alongside fiat-denominated liabilities to improve corporate balance-sheet efficiency. RootstockLabs argues that both could encourage institutions to acquire and retain more BTC.
Bitcoin’s evolving financial utility compared with traditional assets. Source: RootstockLabs report
The report outlines a hypothetical scenario in which institutional Bitcoin holdings double to 7.8 million BTC. If 5% of those holdings earned a 5% annual yield, institutions would collectively generate 19,500 BTC a year. The figure represents potential returns on existing holdings, not a forecast of new Bitcoin demand.
Drawing a comparison to gold, the report argues that successful monetary assets develop additional sources of demand beyond their original role as stores of value. While gold found uses in jewelry and electronics, RootstockLabs sees Bitcoin’s next source of utility emerging through financial markets.
Related: Bitcoin ETF inflows climb to $176M as BTC rebounds above $80K
Asked about the risks associated with Bitcoin’s growing financialization, Tony DiCarlo, director of institutional propositions at RootstockLabs and author of the report, acknowledged the concerns but argued that Bitcoin’s underlying design offers important advantages. He told Cointelegraph:
DiCarlo said borrower defaults, custody failures and legal enforceability remain concerns, while Bitcoin’s volatility adds to leverage risks.
However, he argued that the benefits of financialization could far outweigh those risks, pointing to MARA’s $750 million in Bitcoin-backed loans to help finance a planned power plant acquisition in Ohio. The arrangement allows MARA to retain its Bitcoin holdings while using them as collateral to finance real-world infrastructure.
Bitcoin’s key features for modern finance. Source: RootstockLabs report
DiCarlo also acknowledged that institutional adoption could concentrate Bitcoin holdings among a small number of custodians. While spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds have been a major driver of institutional adoption, “shareholders own shares, not coins,” he said, warning that a few large custodians could end up holding most of the Bitcoin.
Nevertheless, DiCarlo maintained that Bitcoin’s decentralized architecture remains a fundamental advantage, allowing holders to retain control of their assets and enabling financial services with fewer intermediaries, potentially reducing counterparty risks and fees.

Morning Minute: Hedge Funds Left the BTC ETF Trade and Sovereign Wealth Stepped In - Decrypt
text:
Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner. The analysis and opinions expressed are his own and do not necessarily reflect those of Decrypt. And check out our daily news show 'FOMO HOUR' covering all of the top stories and market action.
Every quarter, big institutions have to tell the SEC what they own. Add up those filings from just before Bitcoin’s October 2025 high through the end of June, and the picture is clear: nine hedge funds and banks sold about 68,000 Bitcoin worth of ETF shares over those nine months, roughly $5.4 billion at today’s prices. Millennium, Brevan Howard, Goldman Sachs, D.E. Shaw and five others led the selling. Some trimmed by a third. Some sold everything.
The trade had nothing to do with believing in Bitcoin. You buy the ETF, you simultaneously bet against Bitcoin in the futures market, and you pocket the gap between those two prices. Done right you make money whether Bitcoin rises or falls—as long as the gap beats what you’d earn just parking the cash in Treasury bills.
Before the high, that gap paid 7.9% a year, a full 3.9 points better than T-bills. By late October it paid 4.8%, barely half a point better. After fees and financing, Galaxy’s Alex Thorn figures what’s left is about 1.5 points over cash. Not worth the trouble.
“That arithmetic, not the price, is why the multi-strategy desks left,” he wrote.
You can see it in the futures data too. Both sides of that trade shrank by nearly identical amounts, around 57% each.
Now look at who came in and bought. Morgan Stanley’s wealth management arm. Mubadala. The Abu Dhabi Investment Council. Roughly 2,200 other filers added about 20,000 Bitcoin between them. Hedge funds sold; sovereign funds and wealth managers bought. And the investors too small to file at all—advisers, family offices, regular people—cut their holdings by just 6.6% while the price fell 49%. So Middle America is hodling.
That’s the whole story. The people who were never really Bitcoin investors left. The people who were didn’t flinch.
Since June, the funds have added back 87,000 Bitcoin—this time as straightforward buying, not arbitrage.
The rate picture is turning too. The Fed held Wednesday, but December has quietly softened: a month ago traders put 59% odds on two rate hikes by year-end. Today that’s zero. Expected tightening has been cut roughly in half. Less tightening helps every risk asset.
October’s flows already show the shift. The month was down $907 million at the midpoint. Through Tuesday it’s essentially flat, with $724 million arriving in just the last eight sessions.
The fast money is gone. The believers are left. And that’s the foundation you can build on for a bull market rally…

title: Unlimit Founder Commits $45M to Phase AI Blockchain
text:
Phase’s new network lets smartphone owners earn tokens for validating transactions and sharing internet connections with AI agents.
Phase, a new blockchain that lets smartphone users earn tokens by helping run AI services, has received a $45 million funding commitment from Unlimit founder Kirill Eves.
Phase announced the launch of its blockchain on Thursday alongside Phase Proxy, a service that routes AI agents’ web requests through internet connections shared via smartphones.
Phase has no outside investors, the company told Cointelegraph. Eves’ $45 million commitment covers its first two years of development and provides another two years of runway.
“Websites routinely block or rate-limit automated traffic originating from data centers, even when an agent is acting on a legitimate user request,” Eves told Cointelegraph. “As agents take on more tasks across multiple websites, these restrictions are becoming a significant barrier to their adoption.”
Internet infrastructure provider Cloudflare allows website owners to manage AI traffic. For new domains, its settings block agent and training traffic on pages displaying ads.
Eves founded Unlimit in 2009 and built it into a global payments company. Unlimit said in December 2025 that it served more than 50,000 businesses worldwide.
Related: Cloudflare introduces wallets for AI agents, plans stablecoin payments
Smartphone users can join the Phase network through the Phase app and earn PHASE tokens by validating blocks and sharing their internet connection through the proxy service.
“Current flagship smartphones can deliver approximately 35–45 TOPS [trillions of operations per second] of AI processing performance, depending on the device, allowing them to run smaller open-weight AI models locally,” Eves said.
Related: Tech chief says EU can fend off rogue AI risk: Report
Participation is adjusted based on a device’s battery level and connectivity.
Smartphone users will be able to contribute computing power when Phase launches its AI computing service, planned for November. A second service expected in November will route requests across AI models.
Phase said that it plans to develop its own model and expand to desktops, servers and graphics processing units.
Part of the revenue from these services would fund PHASE purchases on the open market, which would be used to reward node operators.

title: Chainalysis Maps DPRK Crypto Cash-Outs After OFAC Sanctions
text:
The analysis followed US sanctions against 10 people and one entity accused of helping North Korean IT worker schemes fund weapons programs.
Blockchain analytics company Chainalysis mapped a long-running network of Russian intermediaries that helped North Korean IT workers cash out millions of dollars in cryptocurrency.
The US Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned 10 individuals and one entity on Wednesday for supporting North Korean government-run IT worker schemes that it said funded the country’s weapons programs, according to a press release.
Those sanctioned included Russian nationals Ilya Aleksandrovich Boykov and Vitold Viktorovich Obertas. Treasury said Boykov had converted about $3.5 million in crypto for sanctioned company Alis since 2024, while Obertas had handled nearly $2 million in crypto conversions for North Korean officials since January 2025.
In one example, a wallet linked to a North Korean IT worker received regular stablecoin payments, converted them into Ether (ETH) and transferred the funds through consolidation addresses to Boykov, according to Chainalysis’ Wednesday report. North Korean IT workers using false identities to obtain jobs at crypto companies have posed a persistent security threat. title: Mosaic: The Art Hidden In Bitcoin
text:
How generative artist BitArt is transforming sats into a collective visual and musical composition, and why Bitcoin Art Society believes the network could become a permanent medium for contemporary art.
A mosaic is an artwork assembled from fragments. From ancient Roman floors to Byzantine churches, artists have used pieces of stone, glass, and ceramic to construct images that have endured for centuries.
For the generative artist known as BitArt, those fragments are satoshis (or sats), the smallest units of bitcoin.
In Mosaic, a continuously evolving artwork developed through the Bitcoin Art Society (BAS), the numerical properties of satoshis are translated into color and spatial coordinates. Each contribution adds to an expanding composition of pixels resembling digital textiles, early computer graphics, or abstract paintings.
Rather than illustrating bitcoin through familiar iconography, Mosaic treats the network itself as artistic material. Satoshi positions and unspent transaction outputs (UTXOs) become inputs for a rule-based system that determines the artwork’s appearance. BitArt begins with bitcoin’s underlying data and allows an image to emerge.
The approach recalls conceptual artist Sol LeWitt’s proposition that an artwork can exist as a set of instructions rather than a singular handcrafted object. Generative artists such as Vera Molnár and Manfred Mohr similarly explored how mathematical systems and computational procedures could produce visual compositions. Mosaic extends this tradition into an economic network shaped by transactions and human decisions.
The scale is extraordinary. According to BitArt, Mosaic now contains more than 127 million tiles and one billion layers. Viewing every layer at a rate of one per second would take over 30 years.
The project has also expanded into sound. Its musical component draws from the same satoshi data that generates the imagery, translating numerical values into an evolving score. Together, these elements create an audiovisual artwork shaped by bitcoin’s underlying structure and the contributions of its participants.
These experiments form part of the broader ambitions of Bitcoin Art Society, founded by Serge Ajamian and Yara Al Chammaa to support the creation, exhibition, and preservation of digital art on bitcoin.
For Al Chammaa, preservation is particularly personal. Following the 2020 Beirut Port explosion, which destroyed much of the artwork housed in her family’s gallery, she began reconsidering how cultural heritage might survive physical destruction. That experience helped inform BAS’s interest in bitcoin as a potential medium for preserving cultural works beyond the vulnerabilities of physical institutions.
BAS has since presented bitcoin-native digital art internationally, including Mosaic accompanied by live musicians at the Galileo Galilei Planetarium in Buenos Aires. Its inaugural artist residency features BitArt and CyberSea, whose practices investigate generative systems and blockchain-native artistic production.
Yet permanence raises questions beyond the durability of bitcoin’s ledger. Software-based art has long challenged museums to preserve not only underlying materials but also the technologies and experiences through which artworks are encountered. For Mosaic, what constitutes the artwork: the code, the rendered image, the accumulated contributions, or the experience of navigating the system?
At Bitcoin Amsterdam 2026, Mosaic will be presented on the conference’s main-stage LED installation, bringing its intricate visual structures to an architectural scale, similar to BAS’s immersive presentation at the Galileo Galilei Planetarium in Buenos Aires.
Ahead of the event, I spoke with BitArt about the project’s artistic origins, collective authorship, and the possibility of preserving an artwork that may never be finished.
BMAG: You’ve described bitcoin as a time-based transactional medium rather than simply a platform for displaying art. What first led you to recognize its underlying mathematical and economic structures as artistic material, and how did that thinking develop into Mosaic?
BitArt: Bitcoin records the movement of value through a sequence of events secured by computational work, creating a history that becomes increasingly difficult to reverse. What interests me is not just the individual event, but the sequence of events that led to it. In the context of art, this shifts the question from “What is the artwork?” to “What had to happen for the artwork to become what it is?”
With the advent of the Ordinals protocol, it became possible to assign a unique number to every satoshi. This opened up new possibilities.
From there, Mosaic developed almost naturally. I only had to highlight what was already there. Once every satoshi has an assigned ordinal number, it becomes relatively straightforward to determine its position and derive its color or musical parameters through a set of rules.
The interesting part is that these structures emerge from a system driven by human decisions, rather than one designed to produce art.
BMAG: Artists from Sol LeWitt to Vera Molnár have explored how predetermined rules can produce unexpected visual outcomes. In Mosaic, how do your decisions shape the system, and where does bitcoin’s underlying data take over?
BitArt: In a sense, Mosaic continues the tradition of rule-based art explored by LeWitt and Molnár, and builds on the concept of protocol art explored by Holly Herndon and Mat Dryhurst. But it introduces yet another layer: the input is the accumulated result of human decisions within an economic system.
My artistic decisions determine the rules of interpretation, but the underlying data determines the resulting visual and sonic structures.
The rules are deterministic, but the results are not necessarily predictable in practice. I find that tension particularly interesting. The artist creates the conditions under which something can emerge, rather than specifying what it should look or sound like.
BMAG: Participants contribute to Mosaic through their own transactions, becoming part of a composition that no single person controls. Does that make them collectors, collaborators, or something else?
BitArt: I think of authorship as something distributed across several layers.
Perhaps the most interesting aspect is that individual intentions can generate collective structures that nobody intended. Everyone contributes something specific, but the larger composition belongs to the system as a whole.
A participant can be a collector, but also becomes a contributor to the artwork’s evolving structure. The distinction between collecting and creating becomes less clear. Each contribution changes the work, but nobody, including myself, controls the resulting composition.
Authorship becomes less about controlling an outcome and more about establishing the conditions under which it can emerge.
BMAG: You’re developing a system for the upcoming Postmasters exhibition that will allow visitors to speak directly with artworks and receive responses. How does this differ from participating in Mosaic through bitcoin transactions? Are these different forms of communication through computational systems?
BitArt: Yes, both are intentional acts mediated by computational systems, but there is an important semantic distinction.
A contribution to Mosaic through a Bitcoin transaction is a non-verbal gesture that becomes part of a verifiable record. We can establish exactly what happened and how it changed the artwork. The action leaves a trace that the system can process directly.
Speaking to an artwork is different. Natural language must first be interpreted and translated into the formal language the artworks use to communicate.
In the first case, the action produces a verifiable change in the artwork’s state. In the second, it initiates a process of interpretation.
Both are expressions of human intention, but one establishes a computational fact, while the other opens up a space for interpretation.
BMAG: You’ve written about the creative uncertainty that emerges during programming and experimented with the relationship between real time and bitcoin’s block time. How important are unpredictability, chance, and duration to your practice? Has Mosaic produced results that surprised you or challenged your original intentions?
BitArt: I designed the algorithm for Mosaic to be as simple as possible. It’s deterministic, so its results are technically predictable and reproducible. From a technical standpoint, there shouldn’t be any surprises. Nonetheless, the results are full of unexpected and surprising elements.
I think there is an important distinction between something being computationally predictable and our ability to anticipate or comprehend its results.
Currently, Mosaic contains over 127 million tiles and over 1 billion layers. To view all the layers at a rate of one layer per second would take over 30 years. There are many things that have surprised me, and I’m still discovering new ones.
The temporal divergence between real time and Bitcoin’s block time is also interesting to me. Bitcoin evolves according to its own rhythm, independently of how and when we observe it. This introduces another dimension of duration into the artwork.
BMAG: The introduction of sound adds another dimension to Mosaic, with musical compositions generated from the same data that determines the visual structure. What can sound reveal about the underlying system that an image cannot?
BitArt: From the very beginning, Mosaic was built on three fundamental ideas.
The first is the possibility of capturing traces of human intention within a financial, algorithmic system and revealing visual and sonic structures from them.
The second is the development of a formal system in which Mosaic becomes meta-aware, in the sense of being self-referential and introspective, and capable of communicating and collaborating with other artworks.
The third is collective creation. Anyone can contribute to Mosaic and become part of its evolving structure.
Looking at Mosaic from any of these perspectives reveals something different about it. In the case of sound, it reveals melodic, harmonic, contrapuntal, and rhythmic structures that aren’t necessarily apparent in the visual representation.
Yet within the digital realm, the structures underlying the image and the music are closely related, sometimes almost identical. Perhaps the way we think about visual, sonic, and programmatic structures as separate domains is itself a limitation.
BMAG: Your practice has been presented in contexts including the Whitney, ZKM, and ICC Tokyo, institutions with significant histories in digital and media art. Where do you see Mosaic within the broader history of generative and systems-based art? What does working directly with bitcoin make possible that earlier computational media did not?
BitArt: I see Mosaic as part of the tradition of generative and systems-based art, but I’m particularly interested in extending that tradition beyond the generation of images and sound.
I’m currently working on a show at Postmasters gallery in New York City in collaboration with BAS. The show will present Mosaic in communication and collaboration with other artworks.
In principle, any artwork that can be represented digitally can join the conversation, whether it’s Leonardo’s Mona Lisa, Malevich’s Black Square, an artwork inscribed on Bitcoin, or music as diverse as traditional folk songs, Nine Inch Nails’ 34 Ghosts IV, and Ravel’s Boléro.
Through the system I mentioned earlier, these artworks can reference themselves and one another, exchange statements, and initiate collaborations using a machine-readable formal language. What’s particularly interesting is that the audience will also be able to join these conversations by speaking directly with the artworks in natural language.
Historically, discourse about art happened outside the works themselves, in texts, institutions, discussions, and criticism. Artworks remained largely silent objects of interpretation. By giving artworks the formal means to reference one another, reason about themselves and others, and exchange verifiable statements, the project treats discourse itself as artistic material.
Art history normally describes influence retrospectively. Here, through collaborations between artworks, influence becomes operative. Influence becomes something artworks can perform.
Bitcoin introduces another dimension by providing a shared, ordered, and verifiable record of these exchanges and the artworks’ histories of collaboration. Unlike a conventional computational environment, this record can exist independently of any single artist, institution, or platform.
The artwork is no longer simply the result of a process or the process itself. It becomes a participant in an ongoing process of interpretation, communication, and creation.
BMAG: Mosaic has already been presented in immersive environments, including the Galileo Galilei Planetarium in Buenos Aires. For Bitcoin Amsterdam, the work will be adapted for large-scale main-stage LED screens. How does that change the way audiences encounter the work, particularly when its original form is interactive and continuously evolving?
BitArt: The surface of the artwork is not fixed, and it is not what constitutes the artwork. It’s a manifestation of its state at any given time.
I like BAS’s approach of presenting it in intimate settings, large-scale immersive environments, and anywhere in between. Each setting allows the audience to experience a different aspect of the same underlying system.
In an interactive environment, the viewer navigates Mosaic individually, while on large-scale screens, the experience becomes collective. The audience encounters the artwork as it unfolds, rather than exploring it directly.
For the Postmasters show, I’m also developing a physical component that will provide yet another way of experiencing Mosaic.
What interests me is that the artwork can take on very different forms without changing its underlying identity. The presentation changes, but the system that constitutes the work remains the same.

title: Justin Sun's HTX Agrees to Leave UK in Settlement With Financial Watchdog - Decrypt
text:
Crypto exchange HTX is leaving the UK after settling a lawsuit brought by the Financial Conduct Authority over illegal crypto promotions, the regulator said on Thursday.
The FCA said it had secured undertakings in the High Court that HTX, formerly known as Huobi, will not knowingly promote crypto services unlawfully to UK consumers. Huobi Global S.A., the Panama-registered company named as the first defendant, has undertaken not to communicate financial promotions in breach of UK law across HTX's website, apps and social media, according to the court order.
HTX, which names Tron founder Justin Sun as a global adviser, is no longer active in the UK, the regulator said. UK consumers can no longer make deposits, and new UK users cannot sign up.
"Crypto firms should be under no illusion: being based overseas does not put them beyond the reach of UK law," said Steve Smart, the FCA's executive director of enforcement and market oversight. "The message to other firms is clear: follow the rules or face the consequences."
HTX said it had "proactively implemented measures to align with the UK's financial promotion regulations," the Financial Times reported. On its website, the exchange said existing UK customers are blocked from trading and have 48 hours to withdraw their assets before their accounts are closed.
The terms of the settlement are confidential, and it does not amount to an admission of liability or wrongdoing, the FCA said.
The regulator began proceedings against HTX in October 2025, its first enforcement case against a crypto firm under the UK's financial promotion rules, saying the exchange had repeatedly failed to engage with it. The two sides began settlement talks in March, which were extended in June, according to court orders reported by Reuters.
In May, the UK sanctioned Huobi Global S.A. over alleged support for Russia's financial sector, with the government's notice listing HTX as another name for the designated entity.
Two months later, the European Union named Huobi Global in its 21st package of Russia sanctions, accusing it of "significantly frustrating" the bloc's measures and barring EU transactions with the exchange, though stopping short of a full asset freeze. HTX has said Huobi Global S.A. is "distinct from the online HTX exchange."

title: Polygon adds Solana to payment stack linking bank accounts, crypto and payouts
text: Polygon Labs has added Solana to its Open Money Stack, bringing the network into a payments platform that connects bank accounts with crypto transfers and payouts. Businesses can use a single integration to bring money in from bank accounts, move funds across blockchains and pay recipients, Polygon said in a statement shared with The Block. The stack connects Solana with other networks as well, including Polygon, Ethereum and TRON, which was added earlier this month. Businesses can also use it to provide customer accounts and wallets, convert funds and route payments to supported bank accounts, cards, cash services, and crypto wallets, according to Polygon. title: Polygon Extends Its Stablecoin Payments Infrastructure to Solana - Decrypt
text:
Polygon Labs is extending its stablecoin payments infrastructure to Solana, giving businesses on the rival network a single connection to pull money in from bank accounts, move crypto across chains, and pay out to customers and suppliers worldwide.
The company said the expansion brings its Open Money Stack, a bundle of payments tools, to Solana for the first time.
The pitch addresses a persistent headache in crypto payments: sending the tokens is the easy part, but getting money from a bank account into a wallet, converting it and landing it back in a recipient’s bank account typically requires stitching together several providers, each with its own integration and contract.
Open Money Stack collapses that into one technical connection and one commercial relationship, with businesses free to adopt the whole thing or mix individual pieces into their existing systems.
Through the platform, a Solana business can connect bank, card, cash, and crypto funding routes, spin up embedded wallets, route and convert funds across networks including Polygon, Ethereum and Tron, and deliver payouts into banks, cards, or wallets. A remittance provider, for instance, could take dollars from a sender, deliver USDC on Solana, and connect the recipient to a bank payout.
“Every bank and fintech that wants to use crypto faces the same problem: connecting them to the accounts and payment systems its customers already use,” said Sandeep Nailwal, co-founder and CEO of the Polygon Foundation, adding that adding Solana lets more businesses build on the network their customers choose.
Cross-border payments firm Kira is among the first to adopt Solana through the stack, using it to help clients turn stablecoin transfers into dollars in their bank accounts to pay overseas suppliers.
The move reflects Solana’s growing pull as a payments venue, having processed more than $5 trillion in stablecoin volume this year, per the Solana Foundation.
The network recently rolled out an institutional settlement standard with input from J.P. Morgan and went live with its Alpenglow upgrade. For Polygon, the expansion builds on its broader payments push, including its acquisition of crypto-cash firm Coinme.

title: Polygon Expands Open Money Stack to Solana

title: Understanding The Various Bitcoin Per Share Metrics
text:
Bitcoin per share is one of the most important metrics for evaluating a Bitcoin treasury company. It measures how much bitcoin is attributable to each common share. However, there are several ways to calculate this figure, and each method provides different information about the economics of owning the common stock.
Understanding these differences is essential for evaluating a company’s capital structure, measuring accretion, and determining the value attributable to common shareholders.
The simplest metric is raw Bitcoin Per Share (BPS).
BPS = Total Bitcoin Holdings / Common Shares Outstanding
This calculation divides the company’s bitcoin holdings by its existing common shares. It provides a straightforward measure of how much bitcoin is attributable to each currently outstanding share.
The primary limitation is its treatment of potential dilution. A company may have warrants, convertible debt, or convertible preferred stock that could eventually become common shares. Raw BPS only counts existing shares, so it provides an incomplete picture of the potential future share count.
Bitcoin Per Assumed Diluted Share (BPADS) addresses this limitation by incorporating the shares that would exist if all potentially dilutive securities converted into common stock.
BPADS = Total Bitcoin Holdings / Assumed Diluted Shares Outstanding
Because the assumed diluted share count is greater than or equal to the existing share count, BPADS is always less than or equal to raw BPS.
This metric became widely cited beginning in 2024, particularly as Bitcoin treasury companies began using increasingly complex capital structures.
BPADS provides a more conservative view of bitcoin ownership by incorporating potential dilution from outstanding securities. It becomes especially relevant for companies with substantial convertible debt, warrants, or convertible preferred stock.
However, its assumption of full conversion can be overly conservative.
Warrants and convertible debt may never convert if the common stock price remains below their conversion or exercise prices. Perpetual convertible preferred stock may also remain outstanding indefinitely if investors prefer receiving the preferred dividend rather than converting into common equity.
Consequently, BPADS represents a fully diluted scenario rather than a forecast of the actual future share count.
Both BPS and BPADS share another major limitation: they measure gross bitcoin holdings without accounting for senior claims on the company’s assets.
Common equity sits at the bottom of the capital structure. Debt holders and preferred shareholders generally have priority over common shareholders according to their contractual rights.
These senior claims matter because they reduce the assets ultimately attributable to common equity.
Net Bitcoin Per Share (Net BPS) addresses this by deducting the bitcoin equivalent of senior claims from total bitcoin holdings before dividing by the common share count.
Net BPS = (Total Bitcoin Holdings − Senior Claims / Bitcoin Price) / Common Shares
For example, a company with $1 billion in senior claims and a bitcoin price of $100,000 would need the equivalent of 10,000 bitcoin to satisfy those claims.
Those 10,000 bitcoin would therefore be deducted from gross bitcoin holdings when calculating Net BPS.
The denominator can use either existing common shares or an assumed diluted share count. However, the treatment must remain consistent: securities assumed to convert into common stock should have their extinguished senior claims removed from the numerator’s deductions. This avoids counting the same obligation twice.
There are two useful approaches to calculating Net BPS.
The first applies cash and cash equivalents against senior claims before deducting the remaining obligations from bitcoin holdings.
Net BPS = [Bitcoin Holdings − (Senior Claims − Applied Cash) / Bitcoin Price] / Common Shares
Here, applied cash is limited to the amount available to offset senior claims. This method reflects the fact that cash can satisfy obligations, preserving more bitcoin for common shareholders. This is the methodology used by Strategy to compute their mNAV.
The second approach deducts the full value of senior claims from bitcoin holdings and reports cash separately. For example, investors could examine both Net BPS and Cash Per Share. This separation provides a clearer view of the company’s bitcoin exposure alongside its independent cash reserves, at a per-share level.
Both approaches are useful. Including cash produces a more comprehensive measure of residual asset value, while excluding cash makes the company’s bitcoin and cash positions separately visible.
A defining characteristic of Net BPS is its sensitivity to the price of bitcoin.
Raw BPS and BPADS depend on bitcoin holdings and share counts. Net BPS additionally depends on bitcoin’s market price because senior claims are generally denominated in dollars.
As bitcoin appreciates, fewer bitcoins are required to cover a fixed dollar obligation, so more bitcoins remain attributable to common shareholders. When bitcoin depreciates, the opposite occurs.
Net BPS therefore rises with bitcoin’s price and falls when bitcoin’s price declines, assuming fixed senior claims, holdings, and share counts.
This relationship creates both a challenge and an important advantage.
The challenge is that changes in Net BPS over time combine the effects of corporate actions with changes in bitcoin’s market price.
A rising bitcoin price can increase Net BPS even when a company’s financing decisions destroy value for common shareholders. Conversely, falling bitcoin prices can obscure the benefits of genuinely accretive transactions.
This makes directly comparing observed Net BPS figures across different dates an unreliable method of evaluating management’s capital allocation decisions.
However, raw BPS and BPADS are also inadequate measures of economic accretion.
Consider a company issuing debt to purchase bitcoin. Any positive amount of bitcoin purchased with debt increases raw BPS because bitcoin holdings rise while common shares remain unchanged. This holds regardless of the debt’s interest rate or repayment obligations.
Similarly, issuing preferred stock to purchase bitcoin increases raw BPS even if the preferred stock is issued at a substantial discount to par and carries expensive dividend obligations.
These transactions increase gross bitcoin ownership per common share while potentially reducing the residual value attributable to common shareholders.
The proper way to measure economic accretion is to compare Net BPS before and after a transaction while holding the bitcoin price constant.
This isolates the effects of changes in bitcoin holdings, senior claims, cash, and share count.
It reveals whether a corporate action genuinely increases the bitcoin equivalent of the residual assets attributable to each common share.
Perhaps the greatest advantage of Net BPS is its connection to the economic value of common equity. When bitcoin is a company’s primary treasury asset, Net BPS calculated with the appropriate cash adjustment approximates the bitcoin denominated liquidation value attributable to each common share.
(Note: by liquidation value, I mean the value that common stockholders would be entitled to if they liquidated the company, paid off all the claims, and divided the remainder amongst themselves. This has nothing to do with the “liquidation value” associated with leveraged, margin-callable trading positions. Actual recoveries in a real liquidation depend on the precise terms of senior securities, other assets and liabilities, liquidation expenses, and the taxable proceeds realized from asset sales.)
Multiplying Net BPS by the bitcoin price converts this amount into dollars. Investors can then compare that dollar figure with the common stock’s market price to measure the premium or discount at which the shares trade relative to their estimated residual asset value.
This is an advantage that BPS and BPADS cannot offer. Because Net BPS accounts for senior claims, it provides a more direct measure of the assets that ultimately belong to common shareholders, making it the most relevant basis for comparison with the common stock’s market price.
This connection to common equity liquidation value also explains why accretion is best measured through changes in Net BPS at a constant bitcoin price. Holding the price constant isolates the impact of corporate actions on the residual asset value attributable to each common share. And because Net BPS factors in both senior claims and common stock, it accounts for the impact of all possible corporate actions that involve issuance or repurchase of securities interests, while projecting the results of the impact onto the common stock.
Each Bitcoin per share metric serves a distinct purpose.
Raw BPS measures gross bitcoin holdings attributable to existing common shares. BPADS incorporates potential dilution. Net BPS accounts for senior claims and measures the residual bitcoin value attributable to common equity.
For evaluating the capital stack, Net BPS is the most comprehensive of the three. Holding bitcoin’s price constant allows investors to isolate the economic effects of financing transactions and assess genuine accretion. Net BPS provides a direct connection between the company’s balance sheet and the market value of its common stock.

title: Brazil Crypto Rules Leave Questions as Deadline Nears
text:
Brazil’s crypto exchanges face an application deadline on Friday, with costly requirements and unanswered regulatory questions complicating compliance.
Cryptocurrency exchanges operating in Brazil face mounting compliance costs and unanswered regulatory questions ahead of a license application deadline.
Exchanges already operating in Brazil must apply for authorization by Friday to continue operating, but the cutoff date is just the start of a lengthy compliance process.
“Filing is the easy part,” Fabio Cendão, founding partner at Brazilian law firm FCM Law, told Cointelegraph, pointing to challenges such as high capital requirements, complex compliance obligations and recurring audits.
Brazil introduced its crypto regulatory framework in November 2025, setting rules for exchanges, custodians and other virtual asset service providers under the supervision of its central bank, the Banco Central do Brasil (BCB).
Timeline of key deadlines under Brazil’s crypto regulatory framework. Source: Notabene
Brazil ranks as the world’s top country for grassroots crypto adoption, recording $252.5 billion in crypto activity between July 2025 and June 2026, according to Chainalysis.
Crypto platforms that apply on time can continue operating while regulators review their applications, which can take up to two years, according to Cendão.
New entrants must obtain authorization before launching regulated services.
Related: Brazil’s Petrobras uses Cardano to track sustainable aviation fuel, renewable diesel
Companies that miss the deadline must stop providing services within 30 days from Friday, said Marcelo de Castro Cunha Filho, a lawyer at Machado Meyer. From Nov. 6, banks and payment institutions will also face restrictions on conducting crypto transactions with unauthorized providers.
Under Brazil’s new rules, crypto service providers must verify the origin and destination of crypto transfers, including those involving self-custodial wallets. The rules also impose a $100,000 limit on certain international crypto transfers when the counterparty is not authorized to operate in Brazil’s foreign exchange market.
Binance Brazil general manager Thiago Sarandy told Cointelegraph that questions remain over how exchanges should identify self-custody wallets, interpret a $100,000 operational limit and determine minimum transaction-reporting thresholds.
“The lack of clarity creates a risky situation,” Sarandy said, warning that exchanges may report fragmented or inconsistent data to the regulatory authorities, which “puts in jeopardy the oversight capacity.”
Related: France proposes liability for crypto exchanges offering DeFi access
Sarandy said industry association ABCripto had submitted questions to the BCB but had yet to receive answers.
Major global exchanges have filed applications, including OKX, Binance and Coinbase. Meanwhile, Latin American crypto exchange Bitso is ending direct retail services in Brazil through a partnership with local exchange Mercado Bitcoin.
But smaller operators face a steeper challenge. FCM Law’s Cendão said minimum capital requirements range from 10.8 million Brazilian reais ($2 million) to 37.2 million reais, depending on the services offered, alongside technical certification, custody audits and anti-money laundering controls.
He warned that the costs could make compliance unviable for smaller exchanges, potentially increasing market concentration.
Cunha Filho of Machado Meyer also said it was unclear how exchanges that miss the deadline should return crypto to customers who have no accounts with authorized providers or have not agreed to transfer their assets.
The BCB did not respond to Cointelegraph’s request for comment by publication time.

title: USDT on Bitcoin: Can Utexo Compete With Ethereum and Tron?
text:
USDT is coming home to Bitcoin, offering privacy and Lightning-fast payments. But can Bitcoin’s revamped version of Tether compete with stablecoins on ETH and TRON?
Utexo is preparing to bring Tether’s dollar-backed stablecoin back to Bitcoin after a three-year hiatus.
The Dubai-based blockchain startup says it will achieve the integration through RGB, a protocol that keeps asset transaction data off-chain.
The public launch is scheduled for Nov. 28, with Lightning Network support planned for Q1 2027, promising private transfers and fast payments via Bitcoin’s payment network.
But with $300 billion of stablecoin supply already circulating on networks like Ethereum and Tron, why would users want to transact on a slower network that doesn’t offer smart contracts or DeFi? Can it compete with the stablecoin incumbents?
$300 billion of stablecoin supply. Source: DeFiLlama
This isn’t the first time we’ve seen USDT on Bitcoin. It actually began life as a stablecoin on Bitcoin in 2014 through the Omni protocol, but Tether eventually halted issuance in August 2023, citing declining usage.
Tether then announced plans to launch USDT on RGB in August 2025. That didn’t happen, however, Tether subsequently led Utexo’s $7.5 million seed round in March, and the new firm will launch the Bitcoin version of the stablecoin using Tether’s USDT0 protocol.
But if usage of USDT on Bitcoin had declined to the point it was no longer viable the first time around, why would it be more popular now? What has changed since 2023?
Viktor Ihnatiuk, co-founder and chief executive of Utexo, tells Magazine the answer is two-fold: Speed and privacy. Using Bitcoin for the settlement layer, and RGB to keep transaction details off the public blockchain, makes private and fast transactions a reality.
“You can actually achieve any speed you want to achieve,” he says. “Bitcoin is the best blockchain. Lightning is the best technology to scale payments.”
RGB Protocol Documentation. Source: RGB
Utexo grew out of an effort to bring dollar-denominated payments to Bitcoin, and Ihnatiuk says the idea took shape after a conversation with Tether at Bitcoin Prague in 2023.
The company also builds on RGB and Lightning infrastructure developed by ThunderStack, founded by fellow Utexo co-founder Renat Skitsan.
RGB has been in development since 2016 and was designed to let users issue and transfer digital assets through contracts tied to Bitcoin, without recording every transaction detail on its public blockchain.
Rather than making Bitcoin behave like Ethereum, on RGB, the parties validate asset transactions themselves, while cryptographic commitments anchored to Bitcoin help secure the system. That means RGB is a Bitcoin-native protocol rather than a sidechain or rollup.
RGB also works with the Lightning Network, enabling USDT to move through its payment channels without each transfer requiring a base-layer transaction.
“Lightning allows you to do transactions with a dynamic of 100 milliseconds,” Ihnatiuk says. “It’s faster than Solana, it’s faster than Monad, it’s faster than Sui or Aptos. The limitation is only in the brain of people who don’t understand how to scale Bitcoin.”
Bitcoin’s transparency has hampered business adoption, as many firms like to keep their purchases and transaction counterparts confidential.
Ihnatiuk says that rather than compete with networks like Tron on retail transaction volume or Ethereum on decentralized finance, the company believes the combination of secure Bitcoin-based settlement and greater transaction confidentiality will be enough to persuade businesses to make the switch.
Utexo can also selectively disclose relevant transaction information for compliance purposes, Ihnatiuk says, and has procedures for responding to law enforcement requests.
Related: Is Bitcoin kidding itself about the Lightning Network?
2026 institutional investor survey. Source: Coinbase and EY-Parthenon
Utexo opened early access to its USDT Mint product on Oct. 22, allowing verified professional operators, like exchanges, wallets and market makers, to test minting, confidential transfers and redemption on Bitcoin’s Signet test network.
The sandbox gives operators time to test transaction flows and prepare integrations ahead of the public launch at the end of November, after which time Ihnatiuk predicts “everything will become so big.”
But getting existing USDT onto Bitcoin through Utexo Mint involves an additional step. The service locks USDT0 on Arbitrum before minting an equivalent amount of USDT on Bitcoin. Users can redeem their tokens by burning the RGB asset and triggering the release of the corresponding funds on the source network.
Related: Tether says it helped freeze $550M in Iran-linked USDT this year
That means Mint’s security also depends on the mechanisms connecting the networks, not on Bitcoin and RGB alone.
Users need to trust that the USDT0 locked on Arbitrum remains available and can be released when they redeem their Bitcoin-based USDT. Bridges have historically acted like honeypots to hackers, so this architecture introduces additional risk, even if the design attempts to mitigate them.
Utexo says Mint has been audited by Oxorio, although the full audit report is not publicly available.
Utexo has named UniSat as a launch partner, with plans to support USDT transfers and swaps through its wallet, and Ihnatiuk says Utexo is working with 12 over-the-counter network partners and has another 40 in its pipeline.
Ihnatiuk sees opportunities in Bitcoin-native trading and lending, but he says Bitcoin won’t replicate Ethereum’s DeFi ecosystem; its strengths lie in payments and simpler financial arrangements like escrow-based exchanges.
“People who think that it’s possible to replicate Ethereum DeFi on Bitcoin make a huge mistake,” he says. “Bitcoin was never built for DeFi. Bitcoin was always built for payments.”
Another potential use case is helping keep miners on Bitcoin as they could swap BTC for USDT directly on Bitcoin rather than having to move funds to centralized exchanges. That would reduce their exposure to custodial risk and make it easier to automate hedging strategies. “So, for miners, it’s quite beneficial,” he says.
Ihnatiuk is setting an ambitious target for the first year.
“I would love to achieve our minimum milestone of $1 billion USDT on the Bitcoin network in the next 12 months,” he says. “My initial goal is $10 billion. My median goal is $5 billion.”
There is also a question about the benefits for Bitcoin itself. Ihnatiuk says greater USDT adoption will increase miner fee revenue.
“Once USDT comes back to Bitcoin,” he says, “you will get meaningful adoption; all the transactions will come to Bitcoin. So, yeah, miners will be able to make much more.”
So can Bitcoin compete with Ethereum, Tron and other networks as a new home for USDT? Possibly; it just needs to prove there’s a market this time around.

title: Crypto Exchange HTX Agrees To Leave UK In FCA Settlement
text:
HTX is leaving the UK under a confidential FCA settlement that ends its first crypto marketing case, while sanctions from the UK and EU remain in place.
Justin Sun’s HTX has agreed to leave the United Kingdom, closing the Financial Conduct Authority’s first enforcement case against a crypto firm over financial promotions. The regulator announced the settlement today, ending a High Court action that began in October 2025, according to Financial Times reporting.
Under the court undertakings, Huobi Global S.A., the Panama-registered company behind the HTX brand, has promised not to communicate financial promotions that breach UK law across its website, apps and social media channels.
The FCA says the exchange is no longer active in Britain. UK customers cannot deposit funds, and new users cannot register. Existing customers have 48 hours to withdraw assets before their accounts close.
The regulator framed the outcome as a warning. Steve Smart, the FCA’s executive director of enforcement and market oversight, said that being based overseas does not place a firm beyond the reach of UK law.
Smart said that ‘Crypto firms should be under no illusion: being based overseas does not put them beyond the reach of UK law. Our action means HTX is leaving the UK and can no longer target UK consumers. The message to other firms is clear: follow the rules or face the consequences.’
The regulator said HTX had failed to really engage over several rounds of talks of the case. Settlement talks began in March and were extended in June
HTX presents a different account. The exchange says it has put measures in place to align with UK promotion rules.
“We take local compliance requirements seriously and have proactively implemented measures to align with the UK’s financial promotion regulations,” the company said in a statement, according to Reuters.
The settlement terms remain confidential, and the FCA says the deal involves no admission of liability or wrongdoing. Public reporting does not say whether any fine was paid.
In May, the UK sanctioned Huobi Global over alleged support for Russia’s financial sector, listing HTX as another name for the designated entity.
In July, the European Union named Huobi Global in its 21st Russia sanctions package and barred EU transactions with the exchange, stopping short of a full asset freeze. HTX says Huobi Global S.A. is distinct from the online exchange.
Back in August, Kraken clients were briefly locked out of their accounts after receiving tiny amounts of cryptocurrency linked to sanctioned funds in what was known as a dust attack. Kraken said the attacks aimed to trigger compliance checks and spread sanctioned funds across platforms, causing operational disruptions for thousands of users.
Around 12,000 transfers were reportedly sent from a wallet linked to HTX. Kraken’s compliance team quickly restored customer access while retaining the sanctioned funds and working with authorities to prevent further attacks.
